expertInsight: Application Architect is not an exam you book. You earn it by holding four certifications: Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. Once the fourth one is passed, the credential appears on your profile. If you already hold App Builder and Platform Developer I you are halfway there, and the two architect exams are the harder half. Platform Developer I is also the one exam that counts toward System Architect.

whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Application Architect exam for?

personas.label: Platform developers
personas.description: You know Apex and Lightning Web Components and want to show you can design a whole application, not just build parts of it.

personas.label: Senior admins
personas.description: You already design data models, role hierarchies and sharing, and want the architect credential that covers them.

personas.label: Solution consultants
personas.description: You design end-to-end Salesforce solutions and want the credential employers ask for on architect roles.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Application Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: There is no Application Architect exam. The credential is granted once you hold Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. The work is in those four exams, and the two architect ones are considerably harder than the first two.
bullets: No separate exam. The credential is awarded when all four component certifications are active.
Four exams to pass. Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect.
Each has its own format and fee. App Builder and Platform Developer I are the cheaper pair, and the two architect exams cost more. Check each exam guide for the current figures.
It pairs with System Architect. Hold both, and you can apply for the Technical Architect (CTA) review board.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Most people take Platform App Builder first, then Platform Developer I, then Data Architect and Sharing and Visibility Architect. Prepare for each exam on its own terms and use that exam's practice questions.

examFormat.heading: Application Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: There is no Application Architect exam to book. Here is how the credential works:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: The two architect exams in this set are scenario-heavy. A typical question describes a business requirement and asks which data model, sharing design or build approach fits best.
bestWayToPass: Start with Platform App Builder: Declarative building, the data model and automation basics. It is the gentlest of the four.
Then Platform Developer I: Apex, SOQL, triggers and testing. It also counts toward System Architect, so it is useful twice.
Then Data Architect: Data modelling, large data volumes, master data management and migration.
Finish with Sharing and Visibility Architect: Org-wide defaults, role hierarchy, sharing rules and external access.

certificationCard.description: Application Architect is earned, not tested. You get it by holding Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. The practice questions here cover the data model and sharing topics those exams focus on.

keyConcepts.h2: Application Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Data Modelling and Large Data Volumes
blocks.body: From the Data Architect exam. Choose relationships for how the data behaves, not for convenience. A **lookup** is a loose link where either record can exist alone. A **master-detail** link makes the child depend on its parent, inherits the parent's sharing, and allows roll-up summary fields, but it also means deleting the parent deletes the children. **External objects** show data that stays in another system. **Big objects** hold very large volumes of historical data that is written and read but rarely updated. For large tables, keep queries **selective** by filtering on indexed fields, watch for **data skew** where one parent owns too many children, and plan archiving before volumes become a problem.

blocks.heading: Choosing Between Configuration and Code
blocks.body: Salesforce expects you to prefer configuration and reach for code only when configuration cannot do the job. **Flow** covers most automation, including record updates, guided screens and scheduled work. Code becomes the right answer when logic is genuinely complex, when very large volumes need batch processing, or when you must do something Flow cannot. The architect's job is to justify the choice: configuration is cheaper to maintain and survives upgrades, while code brings test requirements, deployment overhead and a maintenance burden. Questions that offer a custom-built option alongside a standard feature usually want the standard feature.

blocks.heading: Designing Record Access
blocks.body: From the Sharing and Visibility exam. Access is built in layers and each layer can only open access further, never close it. **Org-wide defaults** set the baseline, so start as private as anyone needs and open up from there. The **role hierarchy** gives managers access to their team's records. **Sharing rules** share by owner or by field value. **Teams** and **manual shares** cover individual records, and **Apex managed sharing** handles rules that configuration cannot express. External users follow their own rules, with **sharing sets** for Experience Cloud customers. Object and field permissions come from profiles and permission sets, and they are checked before sharing ever applies.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns for Applications
blocks.body: From both architect exams and Platform Developer I. Pick the pattern from the requirement: a synchronous callout when a user is waiting, **Platform Events** or **Change Data Capture** when other systems only need to know something changed, **Bulk API** for large scheduled loads, and **Salesforce Connect** when data should stay in the source system. Keep secrets out of code with **Named Credentials**. Remember the callout limits, 100 per transaction and 120 seconds in total, and move slow work into asynchronous Apex so the user is not kept waiting.

blocks.heading: Build Quality: Testing, Deployment and Governance
blocks.body: Across all four exams, the same expectations recur. Apex needs at least 75% test coverage to reach production, and tests should build their own data and assert real outcomes. Changes move through sandboxes, with source control and the Salesforce CLI or DevOps Center for larger teams. Design for bulk from the start, since code that works on one record and fails on two hundred is the most common defect. Keep an eye on org limits and technical debt, and document the decisions behind the data model and sharing design so the next person can follow them.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Application Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Because this credential is four exams, prepare for each separately. These are the themes that run through all of them.

blocks.heading: Data Modelling Choices
blocks.body: Master-detail for dependent children, roll-ups and inherited sharing. Lookup when records stand alone. External objects when the data should not be copied.

blocks.heading: Record Access Design
blocks.body: Start with the most private org-wide default anyone needs, then open access with the role hierarchy and sharing rules. Only use Apex sharing when configuration cannot express the rule.

blocks.heading: Configuration Before Code
blocks.body: Flow first. Code when logic is complex, volumes are large, or Flow genuinely cannot do it, and be ready to justify the choice.

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns
blocks.body: User waiting means synchronous. Others just need to know means events. Large and scheduled means Bulk API. Should not be copied means Salesforce Connect.

blocks.heading: Large Data Volumes
blocks.body: Keep queries selective, avoid ownership and account data skew, and plan archiving before the table gets big.

nextCertsAfter.heading: What to Do After Application Architect
nextCertsAfter.intro: Application Architect and System Architect together are the prerequisites for CTA:

sampleQuestions.question: An object will hold 40 million records and users need to filter by account. What should the architect plan for?
options: A nightly batch job that copies the records into smaller summary objects
Selective filters backed by indexed fields
A separate Salesforce org created to hold the object's historical records
A restriction preventing users from running any reports on that object
sampleQuestions.explanation: At large volume, queries have to be selective against indexed fields or they time out, so the index strategy is part of the data model.
whyWrong: Summary copies help reporting but do not make the base object queryable.
Splitting across orgs fragments the data and complicates every query.
Blocking reporting avoids the symptom rather than solving it.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a skinny table used for?
options: Holding the audit history of changes made to a given record
Storing records that have been archived from the main object
Faster reads across frequently queried fields
Enforcing validation across a very large set of records
sampleQuestions.explanation: A skinny table holds a narrow set of commonly used fields so reads avoid joining the standard and custom field tables.
whyWrong: Field history tracking records changes.
Archiving is a separate data lifecycle concern.
Validation is unrelated to read performance.

sampleQuestions.question: Users need read access to records they do not own, based on a field value. What should the architect use?
options: Criteria-based sharing rules
Manual sharing applied to each record by its owner after creation
A change to the organisation-wide default so the object is public
A role hierarchy restructured so every user sits beneath one role
sampleQuestions.explanation: Criteria-based sharing opens records automatically according to field values, which is what a data-driven access requirement needs.
whyWrong: Manual sharing does not scale and depends on owners remembering.
Making the object public grants far more access than required.
Flattening the hierarchy breaks the management visibility it provides.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the organisation-wide default for an object determine?
options: The baseline access before any sharing is applied
How many records the object is permitted to contain in total
Which profiles are able to create records on that object
The fields that are visible on the object's page layouts
sampleQuestions.explanation: The org-wide default sets the floor, and sharing rules, hierarchy and manual sharing can only open access above it.
whyWrong: There is no record cap set by the default.
Object create permission comes from the profile or permission set.
Field visibility is governed by field-level security and layouts.

sampleQuestions.question: A requirement can be met with a flow or with Apex. What should decide the choice?
options: Whether the org already contains more flows than Apex classes
Whether the declarative option genuinely meets it
Whether the development team is more comfortable writing Apex code
Whether the requirement was raised by a business or technical user
sampleQuestions.explanation: Declarative build is cheaper to maintain and survives upgrades, so code should be reserved for what configuration cannot do.
whyWrong: Existing counts say nothing about what suits this requirement.
Team preference is not an architectural criterion.
Who asked for it does not determine how it should be built.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main architectural cost of choosing Apex where configuration would do?
options: A reduction in the number of records the object can store
Ongoing maintenance and test coverage obligations
An automatic increase in the org's licence requirements
The loss of the ability to report on the affected object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Code needs tests, review, deployment discipline and someone who understands it years later, none of which configuration demands to the same degree.
whyWrong: Storage is unaffected by implementation choice.
Licensing does not change because logic is coded.
Reporting continues to work normally.

sampleQuestions.question: An integration must notify an external system when an order is approved, without blocking the user. What pattern fits?
options: A synchronous callout made from the approval process itself
A nightly batch job that exports every approved order as a file
A manual export performed by an administrator after each approval
Asynchronous publication of an event
sampleQuestions.explanation: Fire and forget notification suits an event, which decouples the two systems and keeps the user's transaction fast.
whyWrong: A synchronous callout makes the user wait on an external system's availability.
A nightly batch delays the notification by up to a day.
Manual export is neither timely nor reliable.

sampleQuestions.question: When is a synchronous integration the right choice?
options: When the volume of calls is expected to be extremely high
When the external system is known to respond slowly under load
When the user cannot continue without the response
When the receiving system has no availability guarantees at all
sampleQuestions.explanation: Synchronous calls are justified where the answer is needed to proceed, such as a credit check or a real-time price.
whyWrong: High volume favours asynchronous handling.
A slow system is an argument against making the user wait.
Poor availability is a reason not to couple synchronously.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager must see records owned by their whole team. What provides this most simply?
options: The role hierarchy with grant access enabled
Manual sharing applied by team members to their own manager
A sharing rule written for each individual manager in the business
A permission set granting View All on the object concerned
sampleQuestions.explanation: The role hierarchy exists to give managers access to their subordinates' records, and it maintains itself as people move.
whyWrong: Manual sharing depends on individuals remembering every time.
Per-manager rules multiply and go stale as the organisation changes.
View All grants access to every record, far beyond the team.

sampleQuestions.question: What should an architect establish before designing a record access model?
options: How many permission sets the org currently has in place
The number of profiles the previous implementation created
Which reporting tool the business intends to use after go-live
Who must see what, and what must stay restricted
sampleQuestions.explanation: Access design starts from the business rules about visibility and confidentiality, because those determine every structural choice that follows.
whyWrong: Existing counts describe the present rather than the requirement.
Legacy profile counts rarely reflect what is actually needed.
Reporting tooling is downstream of the access model.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does an architect care about test coverage beyond the platform minimum?
options: Coverage determines how many deployments may run each month
The platform refuses to run reports in orgs with low coverage
Tests are what make future change safe
Higher coverage increases the org's available storage allocation
sampleQuestions.explanation: Coverage is not a target to hit once but the mechanism that lets someone change the system later without breaking it.
whyWrong: Deployment frequency is not governed by coverage.
Reporting is unaffected.
Storage is unrelated to test coverage.

sampleQuestions.question: A master-detail relationship is proposed between two objects. What does this commit the design to?
options: Independent sharing settings on each of the two objects involved
Cascade delete and inherited record access
The ability to reparent the detail record at any time afterwards
A limit of one such relationship per object across the whole org
sampleQuestions.explanation: Master-detail ties the child's existence and its sharing to the parent, which is powerful and deliberately rigid.
whyWrong: The detail object inherits the master's sharing rather than having its own.
Reparenting is restricted unless explicitly allowed.
An object may have more than one master-detail relationship.

sampleQuestions.question: When is a lookup relationship preferable to master-detail?
options: When the child must exist independently of the parent
When the child's access must be inherited from the parent
When roll-up summary fields are required on the parent object
When deleting the parent should always delete the children
sampleQuestions.explanation: A lookup leaves the two records independent, which is right when the child is meaningful on its own.
whyWrong: Inherited access is a master-detail behaviour.
Standard roll-up summaries require master-detail.
Cascade delete is a master-detail behaviour.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a deployment pipeline with distinct environments?
options: It allows several administrators to edit production at the same time
It increases the number of API calls the org is allowed to make
It removes the need to write tests for the code being deployed
Change is validated before it reaches production
sampleQuestions.explanation: Separate environments let a change be built, tested and reviewed somewhere it cannot hurt anyone before it goes live.
whyWrong: Concurrent production editing is the risk a pipeline reduces.
API limits are unrelated to deployment process.
Tests remain necessary and are part of what the pipeline runs.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes how the Application Architect credential is obtained?
options: By passing a single scenario-based written examination
By completing a set of Trailhead superbadges and projects
By holding the four prerequisite certifications
By presenting a design to a panel of practising architects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Application Architect is awarded for holding Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect. There is no separate exam.
whyWrong: There is no examination for this credential itself.
Superbadges are not what earns it.
Panel defence is part of the CTA review board, not this credential.
